items.stem: What is the name for "a kidney tubule where blood is filtered and urine is formed"?
items.answer: Nephron
items.markingKey: Nephron: a kidney tubule where blood is filtered and urine is formed.

items.stem: Explain how ultrafiltration happens in the glomerulus.
items.answer: The vessel leaving the glomerulus is narrower than the one entering, creating high pressure that forces water, glucose, salts and urea through the capillary walls into the Bowman's capsule; large proteins and cells stay in the blood.
items.markingKey: high pressure [1]; small molecules forced out [1]; large proteins / cells remain [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why glucose in the urine can indicate diabetes.
items.answer: Normally all glucose is reabsorbed; very high blood glucose means more is filtered than can be reabsorbed, so some appears in urine.

items.stem: The kidneys of an adult filter 150 dm³ of plasma each day and produce 2.0 dm³ of urine. The urea concentration is 0.03 g/100 cm³ in plasma and 2.2 g/100 cm³ in urine. (a) Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed. (b) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in urine than in plasma.

The kidneys of an adult filter 180 dm³ of plasma each day and produce 1.5 dm³ of urine. The urea concentration is 0.03 g/100 cm³ in plasma and 1.9 g/100 cm³ in urine. (a) Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed. (b) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in urine than in plasma. (c) Explain why the concentration of urea increases along the nephron.
items.answer: (a) 99.2% (b) 63 times (c) Water is reabsorbed but urea is not (or little is), so urea becomes more concentrated.

items.stem: The kidneys of an adult filter 170 dm³ of plasma each day and produce 1.6 dm³ of urine. The urea concentration is 0.03 g/100 cm³ in plasma and 2.0 g/100 cm³ in urine. (a) Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed. (b) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in urine than in plasma. (c) Explain why the concentration of urea increases along the nephron.
items.answer: (a) 99.1% (b) 67 times (c) Water is reabsorbed but urea is not (or little is), so urea becomes more concentrated.

items.stem: A patient in Bangkok has kidney failure and is treated by dialysis three times a week, while waiting for a kidney transplant. (a) Describe what happens to glucose and water as filtrate passes along the nephron. (b) Name the blood vessel that carries blood into the kidney and the tube that carries urine to the bladder.
items.answer: (a) All glucose is reabsorbed (active transport) in the proximal tubule; much water is reabsorbed by osmosis along the nephron and collecting duct. (b) Renal artery; ureter.

items.stem: A patient in Karachi has kidney failure and is treated by dialysis three times a week, while waiting for a kidney transplant. (a) Explain why kidney failure is life-threatening if untreated. (b) Describe what happens to glucose and water as filtrate passes along the nephron. (c) Name the blood vessel that carries blood into the kidney and the tube that carries urine to the bladder.
items.answer: (a) Urea and excess salts and water build up in the blood; urea is toxic and the water potential of blood changes, damaging cells. (b) All glucose is reabsorbed (active transport) in the proximal tubule; much water is reabsorbed by osmosis along the nephron and collecting duct. (c) Renal artery; ureter.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "glomerulus"?
options: The tube that carries urine from a kidney to the bladder.
The removal of waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements.
A knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule where ultrafiltration happens.
A kidney tubule where blood is filtered and urine is formed.
items.answer: A knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule where ultrafiltration happens.
items.markingKey: Glomerulus: a knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule where ultrafiltration happens.

items.stem: Which substance is filtered into the Bowman's capsule but is normally completely reabsorbed?
items.answer: Glucose
items.markingKey: All glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.

items.stem: Explain why a person produces more dilute urine after drinking a lot of water.
items.answer: Less water is reabsorbed in the collecting ducts so that excess water is excreted, keeping the water potential of the blood constant.
items.markingKey: less reabsorbed [1]; excess removed [1] [2]

items.stem: Concentrations (g per 100 cm³) in blood plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine: protein: plasma 8.0, filtrate 0, urine 0; urea: plasma 0.03, filtrate 0.03, urine 2.0; glucose: plasma 0.1, filtrate 0.1, urine 0. For each substance, explain the differences between the three values.
items.answer: protein: too large to be filtered, so absent from filtrate and urine; urea: filtered; water reabsorbed but not urea, so concentrated in urine; glucose: filtered but all reabsorbed, so absent from urine
items.markingKey: protein [2]; urea [2]; glucose [2] [6]

items.stem: Describe how the kidney produces urine from blood.
items.answer: Renal artery brings blood; glomerulus — ultrafiltration under high pressure into Bowman's capsule (water, glucose, urea, salts; not proteins/cells); proximal tubule reabsorbs all glucose, some salts, water; loop of Henle / collecting duct reabsorb water; urine (urea, water, salts) to ureter and bladder.
items.markingKey: ultrafiltration [2]; selective reabsorption of glucose [1]; water reabsorption [1]; urine composition / pathway [2] [6]

items.stem: Where does deamination take place?
items.answer: Liver
items.markingKey: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver.

items.stem: Explain why excess amino acids cannot be stored in the body.
items.answer: There is no store for amino acids or proteins, so the excess must be deaminated and the nitrogen removed as urea.

items.stem: Explain why a diet very high in protein increases the amount of urea in urine.
items.answer: More excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver, producing more urea for the kidneys to excrete.

items.stem: A person eats 80 g of protein per day but needs only 50 g. (a) Calculate the mass of excess protein. (b) About 16% of the mass of protein is nitrogen. Calculate the mass of nitrogen that must be removed by deamination each day.

A person eats 150 g of protein per day but needs only 60 g. (a) Calculate the mass of excess protein. (b) About 16% of the mass of protein is nitrogen. Calculate the mass of nitrogen that must be removed by deamination each day.

A bodybuilder in Manila eats a diet very high in protein shakes. A urine test shows high urea concentration. (a) Describe the route taken by urea from where it is made to where it leaves the body. (b) Explain why the body needs some amino acids every day.
items.answer: (a) Liver → hepatic vein → blood → renal artery → kidney (filtered) → ureter → bladder → urethra. (b) To make new proteins for growth, repair, enzymes and antibodies.

items.stem: Explain why carbon dioxide and urea must be excreted.
items.answer: They are toxic in high concentrations: CO₂ lowers blood pH; urea damages cells; they are waste products of metabolism.

items.stem: A person eats 120 g of protein per day but needs only 55 g. (a) Calculate the mass of excess protein. (b) About 16% of the mass of protein is nitrogen. Calculate the mass of nitrogen that must be removed by deamination each day.

The kidneys of an adult filter 180 dm³ of plasma each day and produce 1.8 dm³ of urine. The urea concentration is 0.03 g/100 cm³ in plasma and 2.2 g/100 cm³ in urine. (a) Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed. (b) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in urine than in plasma. (c) Explain why the concentration of urea increases along the nephron.
items.answer: (a) 99% (b) 73 times (c) Water is reabsorbed but urea is not (or little is), so urea becomes more concentrated.

items.stem: A bodybuilder in Hanoi eats a diet very high in protein shakes. A urine test shows high urea concentration. (a) Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the body. (b) Suggest why the bodybuilder is advised to drink more water. (c) Explain why the body needs some amino acids every day.
items.answer: (a) They are deaminated in the liver; the nitrogen-containing part is converted to urea; the rest is used for respiration or stored as glycogen/fat. (b) More water is needed to dissolve and excrete the extra urea in urine. (c) To make new proteins for growth, repair, enzymes and antibodies.

items.stem: What is the name for "a condition in which the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, so blood glucose is not controlled"?
items.answer: Type 1 diabetes
items.markingKey: Type 1 diabetes: a condition in which the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, so blood glucose is not controlled.

items.stem: Explain how negative feedback keeps blood glucose concentration constant.
items.answer: If glucose rises above the set point, the pancreas secretes insulin and the liver stores glucose as glycogen, lowering it; if it falls, glucagon is secreted and glycogen is broken down, raising it.
items.markingKey: rise → insulin → glycogen [1]; fall → glucagon → glucose [1]; returns to set point [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a person with type 1 diabetes must not inject too much insulin.
items.answer: Too much insulin lowers blood glucose too far (hypoglycaemia); brain cells lack glucose for respiration, causing confusion or coma.

items.stem: Two people drank a glucose solution. Both had blood glucose of 4.8 mmol/dm³ at the start. After 45 minutes person A had 7.3 mmol/dm³ and person B had 15.8 mmol/dm³. After 2 hours person A was back to 4.8 but person B was still at 14.3. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose for person B. (b) Suggest which person has type 1 diabetes and explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) 229% (b) Person B: glucose rises much higher and does not return to normal because the pancreas produces little insulin, so the liver does not convert glucose to glycogen.
items.markingKey: (a) (15.8 − 4.8) ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 229% [2] (b) person B [1]; little / no insulin [1]; glucose not converted to glycogen [1] [5]

items.stem: Two people drank a glucose solution. Both had blood glucose of 4.6 mmol/dm³ at the start. After 45 minutes person A had 7.0 mmol/dm³ and person B had 13.8 mmol/dm³. After 2 hours person A was back to 4.6 but person B was still at 12.3. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose for person B. (b) Suggest which person has type 1 diabetes and explain your answer. (c) Explain how blood glucose returned to normal in person A.
items.answer: (a) 200% (b) Person B: glucose rises much higher and does not return to normal because the pancreas produces little insulin, so the liver does not convert glucose to glycogen. (c) The pancreas secreted insulin; the liver (and muscles) converted glucose to glycogen; negative feedback.

items.stem: A 12-year-old in Santiago has been very thirsty, tired and losing weight. A test shows glucose in the urine and high blood glucose. The doctor diagnoses type 1 diabetes. (a) Explain the cause of type 1 diabetes. (b) Explain why the child is losing weight.
items.answer: (a) The insulin-secreting cells of the pancreas are destroyed (by the immune system), so little or no insulin is produced. (b) Without insulin cells cannot take up and use glucose well, so fat and protein are respired instead.

items.stem: A 12-year-old in Cairo has been very thirsty, tired and losing weight. A test shows glucose in the urine and high blood glucose. The doctor diagnoses type 1 diabetes. (a) Explain why glucose appears in the urine. (b) Describe the role of glucagon when blood glucose falls during exercise. (c) Explain why the child is losing weight.
items.answer: (a) Blood glucose is so high that more glucose is filtered than can be reabsorbed in the kidney. (b) Pancreas secretes glucagon; liver breaks glycogen down to glucose, raising blood glucose. (c) Without insulin cells cannot take up and use glucose well, so fat and protein are respired instead.

items.stem: Explain why a person with diabetes is advised to eat regular meals with complex carbohydrates.
items.answer: Starchy foods release glucose slowly, avoiding large rises in blood glucose that the body cannot control without insulin.

items.stem: Explain why blood glucose must be kept within narrow limits.
items.answer: Too high: water leaves cells by osmosis (lower water potential of blood); too low: cells (especially brain) lack glucose for respiration.

items.stem: Omar says: "Insulin breaks down glycogen into glucose." Explain whether Omar is correct.
items.answer: Insulin causes glucose to be converted to glycogen; glucagon causes glycogen to be broken down.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Insulin causes glucose to be converted to glycogen; glucagon causes glycogen to be broken down. [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "widening of arterioles supplying skin capillaries, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost"?
items.answer: Vasodilation
items.markingKey: Vasodilation: widening of arterioles supplying skin capillaries, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost.

items.stem: Explain how vasodilation helps to cool the body.
items.answer: Arterioles supplying skin capillaries widen, so more blood flows close to the skin surface and more heat is lost by radiation.
items.markingKey: arterioles widen [1]; more blood near surface [1]; more heat lost [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why it is harder to keep cool in humid weather.
items.answer: Sweat evaporates more slowly when the air already contains much water vapour, so less heat is removed.

items.stem: A cyclist exercised for 30 minutes and then rested. Data: 0 min: core 37.0 °C, skin 33.0 °C, sweat 0 g; 10 min: core 37.1 °C, skin 34.2 °C, sweat 5 g; 20 min: core 37.3 °C, skin 35.3 °C, sweat 26 g; 30 min: core 37.4 °C, skin 36.0 °C, sweat 37 g; 40 min: core 37.2 °C, skin 35.0 °C, sweat 17 g. (a) Describe the changes in skin temperature. (b) Explain why skin temperature rose although core temperature changed very little.
items.answer: (a) Skin temperature rose from 33.0 to 36.0 °C during exercise then fell to 35.0 °C during rest. (b) Vasodilation: more blood flows through skin capillaries, so skin warms and loses heat; sweating cools by evaporation, keeping core temperature close to 37 °C.

items.stem: Concentrations (g per 100 cm³) in blood plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine: salts: plasma 0.72, filtrate 0.72, urine 1.5; glucose: plasma 0.1, filtrate 0.1, urine 0; protein: plasma 8.0, filtrate 0, urine 0. For each substance, explain the differences between the three values.
items.answer: salts: filtered; some reabsorbed, excess excreted; more concentrated in urine as water is reabsorbed; glucose: filtered but all reabsorbed, so absent from urine; protein: too large to be filtered, so absent from filtrate and urine
items.markingKey: salts [2]; glucose [2]; protein [2] [6]

items.stem: The kidneys of an adult filter 170 dm³ of plasma each day and produce 1.4 dm³ of urine. The urea concentration is 0.03 g/100 cm³ in plasma and 1.9 g/100 cm³ in urine. (a) Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed. (b) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in urine than in plasma. (c) Explain why the concentration of urea increases along the nephron.
items.answer: (a) 99.2% (b) 63 times (c) Water is reabsorbed but urea is not (or little is), so urea becomes more concentrated.

items.stem: A patient in Madrid has kidney failure and is treated by dialysis three times a week, while waiting for a kidney transplant. (a) Describe how ultrafiltration produces filtrate in a healthy kidney. (b) Describe what happens to glucose and water as filtrate passes along the nephron.
items.answer: (a) High pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules (water, glucose, urea, salts) into the Bowman's capsule. (b) All glucose is reabsorbed (active transport) in the proximal tubule; much water is reabsorbed by osmosis along the nephron and collecting duct.

items.stem: How is urea carried from the liver to the kidneys?
items.answer: Dissolved in blood plasma
items.markingKey: Urea is soluble and transported in plasma.

items.stem: Aisha says: "Urea is produced when the kidneys break down proteins." Explain whether Aisha is correct.
items.answer: Urea is produced in the liver by deamination of excess amino acids.

items.stem: Zara filled identical test tubes with water at 70 °C, wrapped them in different numbers of layers of cotton wool (as a model of fat or fur insulation) and measured the temperature drop over 10 minutes. Results table. Number of layers of insulation: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Temperature drop / °C, trial 1: 22, 8.7, 10.2, 8, 6.8; trial 2: 23.3, 14.1, 9.6, 7.7, 6.9; trial 3: 23.1, 13.8, 9.5, 7.8, 6.5. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 with 1 layers (8.7 °C); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Use a lid on each tube to reduce heat loss from the top.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 1 with 1 layers identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) Any one from: use a lid on each tube to reduce heat loss from the top; use a data logger to record temperatures continuously; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the number of layers of insulation (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: A patient in Santiago has kidney failure and is treated by dialysis three times a week, while waiting for a kidney transplant. (a) Explain why kidney failure is life-threatening if untreated. (b) Describe how ultrafiltration produces filtrate in a healthy kidney.
items.answer: (a) Urea and excess salts and water build up in the blood; urea is toxic and the water potential of blood changes, damaging cells. (b) High pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules (water, glucose, urea, salts) into the Bowman's capsule.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "a condition in which the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, so blood glucose is not controlled"?
items.answer: Type 1 diabetes
items.markingKey: Type 1 diabetes: a condition in which the pancreas does not produce enough insulin, so blood glucose is not controlled.

items.stem: A student in Santiago states: "Glucagon and glycogen are the same thing." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Glucagon is a hormone; glycogen is a storage carbohydrate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Glucagon is a hormone; glycogen is a storage carbohydrate. [2]

items.stem: Two people drank a glucose solution. Both had blood glucose of 4.7 mmol/dm³ at the start. After 30 minutes person A had 7.2 mmol/dm³ and person B had 13.5 mmol/dm³. After 2 hours person A was back to 4.7 but person B was still at 12.0. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose for person B. (b) Suggest which person has type 1 diabetes and explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) 187% (b) Person B: glucose rises much higher and does not return to normal because the pancreas produces little insulin, so the liver does not convert glucose to glycogen.
items.markingKey: (a) (13.5 − 4.7) ÷ 4.7 × 100 = 187% [2] (b) person B [1]; little / no insulin [1]; glucose not converted to glycogen [1] [5]

items.stem: A 12-year-old in Singapore has been very thirsty, tired and losing weight. A test shows glucose in the urine and high blood glucose. The doctor diagnoses type 1 diabetes. (a) Explain why glucose appears in the urine. (b) Describe how type 1 diabetes is treated. (c) Describe the role of glucagon when blood glucose falls during exercise.
items.answer: (a) Blood glucose is so high that more glucose is filtered than can be reabsorbed in the kidney. (b) Regular insulin injections (or pump), monitoring blood glucose, controlling carbohydrate intake and exercise. (c) Pancreas secretes glucagon; liver breaks glycogen down to glucose, raising blood glucose.

items.stem: Explain why temperature control is an example of negative feedback.
items.answer: A change from 37 °C is detected by the hypothalamus, which triggers responses that reverse the change and return temperature to the set point.

items.stem: A student in Madrid states: "Blood vessels move closer to the skin surface when we are hot." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Blood vessels do not move; arterioles dilate so more blood flows through capillaries near the surface.
